title: What Garmin recovery data means for lifters
description: Garmin recovery metrics can be useful for strength training, but only if they are translated into choices you can actually use in the gym.
author: Sundee Fundee Team
body:
Garmin users already have access to a lot of recovery context: sleep scores, stress, body battery, heart rate trends, and workout history. The hard part is not gathering the data. It is deciding what to do with it.

## Recovery metrics are decision inputs

A good recovery metric should help answer a simple question: should today be a push day, a maintenance day, or a pull-back day? If the answer is always the same no matter what the data says, then the data is not helping.

## What to watch for

Look at more than one signal. Poor sleep plus elevated stress plus soreness is a different situation than one weird metric after an otherwise solid week. Strength training responds better to trend interpretation than to a single isolated number.

## Make the data actionable

The most useful workflow is to translate recovery context into one of a few clear options: push, hold steady, or modify the session so it stays productive. That means adjusting load, volume, exercise choice, or session intent without abandoning the week.

If you train with an iPhone, the cleanest path is to use Apple Health as the hub for recovery signals, then focus on the training decision. Start here: [Apple Health strength training app](/apple-health-strength-training-app).

The goal is not more dashboard clutter. It is better decisions when the barbell meets the body you actually brought into the gym.
bestFor: Garmin users who want recovery scores translated into actual lifting choices.
